subject: ranef() vs. predict() for colext models

messages.author: d3fd439c2e48caf1
messages.subject: ranef() vs. predict() for colext models
parts:
Hi Richard, Andy, et al.

Can someone enlighten me to the differences between outputs of predict() and ranef() for colext models? 

I've seen it referenced several times here and, in reading the manual (but not too far into the sources cited), I do like the idea of obtaining estimates of the latent occupancy state of sites in which a species was not detected.

I've been comparing site-specific estimates of psi from a two-season model and my initial impression was that the ranef() distributions are driven solely by the detection part of the colext model.  This agrees with what I think of as the latent occupancy state of a site: observable when detected at least once but not when undetected (though estimable).

Two observations gave me this impression:
1) if a site was ever occupied it had a value of 1 using ranef() vs. a high probability (e.g. 0.8) using predict()
2) if observations were "forced" to all 0s (never detected) or 1s (detected >= once) and the pformula of the model set to a constant (pformula=~1), ranef() produced values of only 1 or 0 (or ever, ever so slightly larger than 0)

However, using real data as in observation 1, I've  tried adjusting covariates (or omitting them altogether) in other parts of the model (e.g. psi, gamma, epsilon) while keeping the pformula the same and the ranef() results will vary (though still producing 1s for sites with >= 1 detection), so probabilities are dependent on other parts of the model (as indicated in the manual; Pr(N=k|y,psi,gamma,epsilon,p).  I just don't understand how (and, to be honest, why) the latent state is dependent on anything other than y and p.

I'd like to use these posterior distributions from ranef() when appropriate, I just want to be sure when is most appropriate.

My deepest gratitude for your continued development of the unmarked package and for maintaining this group!

Giancarlo

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] ranef() vs. predict() for colext models
parts:
Dear Giancarlo,
 
Take a look at the algebra of the model. The occupancy model you're fitting is the following (I write the single-season model, because the issue applies equally in single-season and multi-seasons; also, I drop indices):
 
1. z ~ Bernoulli(psi)            
2. y ~ Bernoulli(z * p)
 
Eq. 1 is the description of the latent occupancy state (z) as a function of the occcupancy parameter (psi), and eq. 2 is the description of the relationship between the observed detection/nondetection datum (y) and the latent state (z) and detection probability (p).
 
Now here's the essential difference between predict() and ranef():
predict() gives you an estimate of psi for each site, while ranef() gives you an estimate of z for each site (z_hat; hat for "estimate"). psi_hat is the expected probability for a site to be occupied, given any site covariates. z_hat is your best guess at the occupancy state ("occupied" or "not occupied"), given the observed data (y), the expected occupancy (psi_hat), detection probability and the number of surveys made at that site.
 
Hence, whenever y=1 for one of the reps at a site, z_hat is equal to one. AND, if your model is a good one, it will also yield a high occupancy probability for that site.
 
In contrast, whenever a species was never observed at a site (i.e., all y=0), then z_hat will be higher (a) when the expected occupancy probability for that site is higher, (b) when p for that site is lower and (c) when there are fewer rep surveys.
 
All this can be put in algebra, but this is an attempt to describe things (mostly) in words.
 
Kind regards  -  Marc

messages.author: d3fd439c2e48caf1
messages.subject: Re: ranef() vs. predict() for colext models
parts:
Thank you, Marc.  That helps clarify things for me. 

My main motivation for getting a better grasp on the differences between predict() vs. ranef() is a desire to (sometimes) estimate past colonization/extinction patterns in a more robust way (i.e. accounting for unobserved occupancy states) than using naive occupancy/colonization/extinction.

In this pursuit, I've been generally uncomfortable with interpreting site-level gamma or epsilon probabilities generated by predict() in light of site-level predictions of psi.  Even with what appears to be a good model, I often have the combination of either

1) sites with high (e.g. > 0.8) predicted psi also having a high predicted gamma or
2) sites with low (e.g. < 0.2) predicted psi also having a high predicted epsilon

Related to combination 1, Richard noted in another post that "all [this] means is that in the rare case that *a* site with those covariate values is unoccupied (Z=0), it is very likely to be colonized." 

In nailing down colonization and extinction in a site, it sounds like ranef() may get me closer to an interpretation of what *did* happen compared to what *could* happen via predict()....  but I welcome anyone to correct my impressions!

Thanks again, Marc, and to all who contribute here.

Giancarlo

messages.subject: AW: [unmarked] Re: ranef() vs. predict() for colext models
parts:
hi Giancarlo,

 

not sure whether the probabilities underlying the dynamics are more or less informative about a population than are the realized numbers of colonizations and extinctions.

 

Re. the probability of occurrence at a site where a species was never observed, you can also read page 97 and following pages in the occupancy book.

 

Regards  ----  Marc
